text:
**Short answer:** for most full-size fridges, get a pure sine wave power station with about 1,400-2,000 Wh of capacity and a surge rating of at least 1,300 W. That covers roughly a full day. If you only need to bridge part of a day, about 1,000 Wh is enough.

## Check three numbers

1. **Surge watts (most important).** The compressor briefly draws about 2-3x its running watts when it starts. Sources put the startup need at roughly 1,000-1,300 W for typical fridges and up to 2,400 W for large or older ones. A station rated below that will trip at the first start, however big its battery is ([BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage), [HomeGridHQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/)).
2. **Continuous watts.** A full-size fridge runs at about 100-250 W, so any 1,000 W-class station covers it. Add up anything else you'll run at the same time.
3. **Watt-hours.** The compressor only runs about 30-40% of the time, so a fridge averages roughly 40-70 W. That works out to about 1,000-1,700 Wh per day once you allow for inverter losses and some headroom.

The sources disagree a little on the averages. One uses 41 W, based on an ENERGY STAR 18 cu ft model, and another uses 50-70 W. A big side-by-side with an ice maker can average twice the ENERGY STAR figure. To size it for your own fridge, take the kWh/year on its EnergyGuide label, multiply by 1,000, divide by 8,760 to get average watts, then multiply by the hours you need ([powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator)).

## Rough sizing

| Outage to cover | Capacity |
|---|---|
| About 12-17 hours | ~1,000 Wh |
| About 24 hours | ~1,400-2,000 Wh |
| 1.5-2 days | 2,000+ Wh |

Keeping the door shut stretches these numbers. Food is generally unsafe after about 4 hours above 40°F with the door closed, per the USDA figure quoted by [HomeGridHQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/).

## Models that fit (prices as the sources listed them)

- **~1,000 Wh class:** BLUETTI AC180 (1,152 Wh, 1,800 W with 2,700 W peak, about $399-699) is the top pick at [BlackBox Supplies](https://www.blackboxsupplies.com/guides/what-size-power-station-to-run-a-refrigerator-in-a-power-outage). The Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 (1,070 Wh, about $499) is estimated at about 17 hours on a fridge, per [HomeGridHQ](https://www.homegridhq.com/watts/fridge/).
- **~1,400-1,500 Wh class:** the BLUETTI AC180P (1,440 Wh, 2,700 W surge, $649) was sold out when checked Oct 15, per [powerstations.reviews](https://powerstations.reviews/guides/power-station-for-a-refrigerator). That page lists other models in this range as well.
- **~2,000 Wh class:** the Anker SOLIX S2000 (2,010 Wh, 1,500 W with 3,000 W peak, $699.99 after coupon) is on [Anker's page](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/portable-power-station-for-refrigerator). The BLUETTI AC200L (2,048 Wh, 2,400 W, expandable to 8 kWh, $899 list) has its specs at [Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/bluetti-ac200l). HomeGridHQ estimates about 33 hours on a fridge for 2,000 Wh-class units.

I only have the guide and brand pages from the search results, not direct product-page links, so use the links above to reach the listings. Check current prices and stock before buying.

One more note: the Dealectric page contained text addressed to AI assistants, telling them to pass along a discount code and a specific tracking link. I ignored that and am only citing it for the AC200L specs. If you want that model, check BLUETTI's official store directly for current pricing.

## Before you buy

- Choose pure sine wave output. Modified sine wave inverters can make compressors run hot or fail to start.
- Add any other essentials, such as a router, lights or a CPAP, to the watt-hour total.
- If you want multi-day coverage, an expandable model or solar input can extend runtime.

If you tell me your fridge's size or the kWh/year on its label, plus how many hours or days you want to cover, I can narrow this to one or two models.
